reranked_evidence.snippet: # Omicron, Delta, Alpha, and More: What To Know About the Coronavirus Variants. A quick guide to the coronavirus variants that have been top-of-mind. Since the beginning of the pandemic, we’ve seen a number of prominent variants, including Alpha, Beta, Delta, and Omicron. This is especially true if a new variant is more aggressive, highly transmissible, vaccine-resistant, able to cause more severe disease—or all of the above, compared with the original strain of the virus. Below is a list of—and information about—some of the variants that have been top-of-mind. While the original Omicron strain (BA.1) is no longer circulating, Omicron subvariants are now driving most of the country’s SARS-CoV-2 infections. The original strain of Omicron was more transmissible than Delta was. **How contagious is it?** It’s estimated that Delta caused more than twice as many infections as previous variants—in Connecticut, it was estimated to have been 80 to 90% more transmissible than the Alpha variant.

reranked_evidence.snippet: # The COVID-19 Omicron Variant. ## What Is the Omicron Variant? In November 2021, the World Health Organization (WHO) first identified the Omicron mutation of the COVID-19 virus as a variant of concern. Since then, several sub-variants of Omicron have surfaced, including BA.2, BA.3, BA.4, and BA.5. By the summer of 2022, the BA.5 variant was the most dominant strain in the US. The BA.5 and BA.4 variants appear to be the most contagious types of COVID-19 so far, according to the CDC. In January of 2023, a new Omicron variant called XBB.1.16 was reported and labeled as “one to watch” by the WHO. Your chances of getting any variant of COVID-19 are greatest if you haven't gotten the COVID-19 vaccine. It's still possible to get the virus if you've been vaccinated (breakthrough infection), but your symptoms should be milder and your chances of having to go to the hospital are much less.

reranked_evidence.title: The Omicron variant of COVID-19
reranked_evidence.snippet: 5.   The Omicron variant of COVID-19. # The Omicron variant. Omicron is a variant of the SARS-CoV2 virus that causes COVID-19. As of mid-March 2022, omicron has become the main variant in the United States and worldwide. Omicron usually causes less severe disease than earlier versions of COVID-19, such as the alpha and delta variants that spread throughout the world in 2020 and 2021. Omicron is the most transmissible variant so far, which means it spreads faster and easier than other variants. This is one of the reasons that the World Health Organization (WHO) and the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) classified it as a “variant of concern”in November 2021. The most common of these are BA.1, BA.1.1 and BA.2. Omicron BA.1 and BA.1.1 are still the most common subvariants in the United States. As of mid-March 2022, omicron BA.2 was the cause of almost 1 in 4 new infections in the United States.

Following the original B.1.1.529 variant, several subvariants of Omicron have emerged, including: BA.1, BA.2, BA.3, BA.4, and BA.5. JN.1 went on to spawn multiple notable sublineages, including KP.3.1.1 and XEC in 2024, and LP.8.1, NB.1.8.1, and XFG in 2025.
